Extra East answer key

All 152 questions in Extra East, grouped by the study deck's sections. Each shows its choices in alphabetical order with the right one ticked, and the rule behind it. Names, numbers and times the game fills in during a run show in brackets, such as [station] or [time].

Definitions · Superiority & movement · Train orders · Signals & whistles · Semaphores · Yard limits · Track warrants · GCOR crew & speed · Signals run: at each signal

Definitions 23

1 · 1949 run, on the road · 1949 Standard Code · Definitions

Restricted speed

A bulletin says to run at restricted speed over a bridge being repaired. Under the Standard Code that means…

  • Half the maximum authorized speed
  • Not over 15 MPH, prepared to stop at the next signal
  • Not over 20 MPH
  • Proceed prepared to stop short of train, obstruction or switch not properly lined, and look out for broken rail

The Standard Code gives no mph figure. GCOR 6.27 adds half the range of vision and 20 MPH.

2 · 1949 run, on the road · 1949 Standard Code · Definitions

Approach signal

A fixed signal a mile out warns you of the home signal at the next interlocking. What is it called?

  • A block signal
  • A train order signal
  • An approach signal
  • An interlocking signal

Standard Code: an approach signal is a fixed signal used in connection with one or more signals to govern the approach to them.

3 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 5

One time on the schedule

The time-table shows only one time for No 1 at Cobb. Unless marked otherwise, that is its…

  • Arriving time
  • Leaving time
  • Meeting time
  • Time to be in the clear

Rule 5: not more than two times are given for a train at a station. One time is the leaving time; two times are arriving and leaving.

4 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Definitions

A section

The operator says No 2 is running in two sections today. What is a section?

  • A length of track between two signals
  • A train running extra over part of the line
  • One of two or more trains running on the same schedule
  • Part of the time-table for one subdivision

Standard Code: a section is one of two or more trains running on the same schedule, displaying signals or for which signals are displayed.

5 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Definitions

Main track and siding

Your train is on the siding here. How does the Standard Code define a siding?

  • A main track used in one direction
  • A track auxiliary to the main track for meeting or passing trains
  • A track used only for switching
  • Any track off the main

Standard Code: a siding is a track auxiliary to the main track for meeting or passing trains. The main track extends through yards and between stations and is used by time-table, train order or block signals.

6 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Definitions

Single track

Ashby to Hollis is single track. What does that mean?

  • A main track used by trains in both directions
  • A main track with one siding
  • A track used in one direction only
  • Any track outside a block system

Standard Code: single track is a main track upon which trains are operated in both directions.

7 · 1949 run, at a station · TT&TO primer · What is TT&TO

After the operators

The old Cobb operator says his job is going away. What replaced TT&TO on lines like this?

  • Automatic train stop
  • Longer time-tables
  • More train order offices
  • Track warrants and DTC given by radio, and CTC where traffic paid for it

TT&TO lasted about 150 years, to nearly the 1980s. Radio-delivered Direct Traffic Control and track warrants replaced the agent-operators; CTC and interlockings went in where traffic paid for them.

8 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Definitions

An interlocking

West of Granite the line crosses another railroad under an interlocking. What is an interlocking?

  • A block with automatic signals
  • A siding with a switch at each end
  • Any signal with two heads
  • Signals and appliances connected so their movements must follow in proper sequence

Standard Code: an interlocking is an arrangement of signals and signal appliances so interconnected that their movements must succeed each other in proper sequence. It may be worked by hand or automatically.

9 · Modern run · GCOR · Glossary

Current of traffic

What is the current of traffic on this double track?

  • The direction of the steepest grade
  • The direction the dispatcher sets for each warrant
  • The direction trains move on each main as the rules specify: eastward on Main 1, westward on Main 2
  • Whichever way the last train went

GCOR: current of traffic is the movement of trains in one direction on a main track, as specified by the rules. Double track is two mains with the current one way on one and the opposite way on the other.

10 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · Glossary

A sign with a D

A signal ahead in dark territory carries a D on its mast. What is it?

  • A detector signal you must inspect
  • A distant signal, governing the approach to the signal or interlocking ahead
  • A dwarf signal for sidings
  • A signal you may pass at restricted speed without stopping

A distant signal is outside a block system and governs the approach to a block signal, interlocking signal or switch point indicator. It does not indicate track conditions between itself and that signal. In the signals guide, a P plate marks a detector and a G plate a grade signal.

11 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · Glossary

A switch marked V

You must trail through a switch whose bowl is painted yellow and marked V. What will it do after your train passes?

  • Lock in the reverse position
  • Spring back to its original position
  • Stay where your wheels forced the points
  • Throw itself to normal after a delay

A variable switch stays where the points were forced when trailed through. A spring switch returns to its original position.

12 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · Glossary

Into CTC

Past Ironton the line enters CTC. What authorizes your movement there?

  • Block signal indications, set by the control operator at control points
  • The yardmaster's radio OK
  • Time-table superiority
  • Your track warrant, extended to Ironton

GCOR: CTC is a block system that uses block signal indications to authorize train movements. Control points are absolute signals controlled by a control operator.

13 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · Glossary

DTC territory

A neighboring subdivision runs under DTC. How is authority given there?

  • By block signal indications
  • By time-table and train order
  • By track warrant boxes
  • The dispatcher authorizes occupancy of named blocks, marked by Begin and End block signs

GCOR: in DTC the train dispatcher authorizes occupancy of a DTC block, a length of main track named by wayside signs reading Begin and End block, and by milepost in the time-table.

14 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · Glossary

Interlocking limits

You cross the other railroad at grade at Granite under an interlocking. Where do its limits run?

  • A quarter mile each side of the crossing
  • Between the first and last switches
  • Between the outer opposing absolute signals
  • From the tower to the distant signal

GCOR: interlocking limits are the tracks between the outer opposing absolute signals of an interlocking.

15 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · Glossary

Clearance point

You leave the rear car in the siding at Hollis. Where must it stand?

  • Anywhere past the switch points
  • At the station sign
  • Clear of the clearance point, where a person riding the side of a car can pass equipment on the next track
  • Within one car length of the switch

GCOR: the clearance point is the location closest to a switch where it is safe for equipment, and a person riding the side of equipment, to pass equipment on an adjacent track.

16 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · Glossary

A reverse move

Your warrant says Proceed from Granite to Hollis, and you need to back up 200 feet. What is that in GCOR terms?

  • A reverse movement, opposite the authorized direction, which needs permission
  • A shove move, allowed under any warrant
  • A work move under Box 4
  • Movement against the current of traffic

GCOR: a reverse movement is a movement opposite the authorized direction. Box 2 is one direction only; backing up needs permission.

17 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · Glossary

Yard or yard limits?

Are the Ironton yard tracks and the Ironton yard limits the same thing?

  • No: the yard is the tracks off the main; yard limits are a portion of main track
  • No: yard limits are the yard tracks only
  • Yes, two names for the same tracks
  • Yes, when a yardmaster is on duty

GCOR: a yard is a system of tracks other than main tracks and sidings. Yard limits are a portion of main track designated by signs and time-table or bulletin.

18 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · Glossary

What makes a train

Your engine runs light from the yard to the main. Under the GCOR, when is it a train?

  • Only when it has cars
  • Only with a full crew
  • When it displays a marker and is authorized to operate on a main track
  • Whenever it moves

GCOR: a train is one or more engines coupled, with or without cars, displaying a marker, and authorized to operate on a main track.

19 · Yard job · GCOR · Glossary

The spring switch

The cut trails through the spring switch at the end of the yard track. After the last car has passed, where are the points?

  • Back in their original position: a spring returns them after they are trailed through
  • Half open, until the next movement
  • Locked in the reversed position
  • Where the wheels forced them, until someone lines them back

GCOR glossary: on a spring switch a spring returns the points to their original position after they are trailed through. A variable switch, marked V or with a yellow bowl, leaves them where they were forced.

20 · Yard job · GCOR · Glossary

From Main 1 to Main 2

You cross from Main 1 to Main 2 through two switches joined by a short track between the mains. What is that connection?

  • A controlled siding
  • A crossover
  • A dual control switch
  • A spring switch

GCOR glossary: a crossover is a track connection between two adjacent tracks, consisting of two switches, intended to be used primarily for crossing over from one track to the other.

21 · Yard job · GCOR · Glossary

Working limits on the spur

A track foreman has working limits on the Kestrel Feed spur while his men replace ties. How may the job move inside those limits?

  • At restricted speed, not over 20 MPH
  • Freely: the spur is not main track
  • Only as permitted by the employee in charge of the working limits
  • Only with a track warrant from the dispatcher

GCOR glossary: working limits are a segment of track within definite boundaries on which movements may be made only as permitted by the employee in charge.

22 · Yard job · GCOR · Glossary

Clear on track 2

You set the cars on track 2. Where must the last car stand?

  • Anywhere, as long as the switch is lined back
  • At least one car length from the switch
  • Clear of the clearance point: where it is safe for equipment, and a person riding the side of equipment, to pass on the adjacent track
  • Just past the switch points

GCOR glossary: the clearance point is the location closest to a switch where it is safe for equipment, and a person riding the side of equipment, to pass equipment on an adjacent track.

23 · Yard job · GCOR · Glossary

The switch at the CP

The switch at CP Ironton East is power-operated from the control operator's machine, but it also has a hand lever. What is it?

  • A dual control switch
  • A spring switch
  • A variable switch
  • An electric switch lock

GCOR glossary: a dual control switch is a power-operated switch, moveable point frog, or derail that can also be operated by hand.

Superiority & movement 22

24 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule S-83

Before leaving Ashby

Ashby is your initial station and a register station. What must you find out before Extra 812 East leaves?

  • That the block ahead shows clear
  • The dispatcher's OK on a track warrant
  • Whether all extras on the division have reported clear
  • Whether all superior trains that are due have arrived or left

Rule S-83: a train must not leave its initial station until it has been ascertained whether all superior trains due have arrived or left. Register stations are designated by time-table, and the train register there records the arrival and departure of trains.

25 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 73

Reading the time-table

No 21 is a second-class freight. Your train is an extra. Which is superior?

  • Neither; the first to reach a siding decides
  • No 21: extra trains are inferior to regular trains
  • Your extra, being eastward
  • Your extra, since it has no schedule to keep

Rule 73: extra trains are inferior to regular trains. Rule 72: first class is superior to second, second to third.

26 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 84

Ready to go

The register shows no superior train due. The engineer has steam up. When may he start the train?

  • After whistling — — o —
  • As soon as the brake test is done
  • At once, since extras have no schedule
  • When a proper signal is given

Rule 84: a train must not start until a proper signal is given.

27 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 20

Two green flags

No 2 went by with two green flags on the front of the engine. What do they tell you?

  • Another section of No 2 follows on the same schedule
  • No 2 has right over all trains
  • No 2 is running late
  • The track ahead is clear for two blocks

Rule 20: all sections except the last display two green flags, and two green lights at night. A section is one of two or more trains running on the same schedule, so Second 2 runs on No 2's schedule and you keep clear of it too. The time-table now shows it.

28 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule D-71

Onto double track

East of Hollis the line is double track. On two or more tracks, how is a train superior?

  • By class or direction
  • By direction only
  • By right or class only; direction no longer counts
  • By right, class or direction, as on single track

Rule D-71: on two or more tracks a train is superior by right or class only. Right is conferred by train order, class by time-table, and right is superior to class. The S- rules are the single-track versions.

29 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule S-87

Too close to [train]

You got into the siding at [station] only [n] minutes ahead of [train]'s time there. By how much must an extra clear the time of an opposing regular train?

  • Any margin, as long as it is in the clear
  • Not less than 2 minutes
  • Not less than 5 minutes
  • Only to the leaving time

Rule S-87: extras must clear the time of opposing regular trains by not less than 5 minutes unless otherwise provided. The TT&TO primer quotes 10 minutes.

30 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 86

[train] was close behind

[train] was due to leave the station behind you before you were in the clear at [station]. When must an inferior train running ahead of a superior train be clear?

  • 5 minutes before the superior train is due at the station ahead
  • At the superior train's arriving time at the station ahead
  • When the superior train comes in sight
  • When the superior train is due to leave the next station in the rear where time is shown

Rule 86: unless otherwise provided, the inferior train must be clear at the time the superior train is due to leave the next station in the rear where time is shown.

31 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 99

Hot box

Smoke from a journal on the ninth car. The engineer stops Extra 812 East on the main track to cool and repack it, about 15 minutes. Trains may come up behind you or against you. What protection do you give the train?

  • Flagman drops a lighted fusee while the train stands Dropping fusees at intervals protects a moving train.
  • Flagman goes back with two torpedoes and, when necessary, lighted fusees; the front is protected the same way when necessary
  • Leave the marker lamps lit; that is protection enough
  • No protection; the stop is short

Rule 99: a stopped train that may be overtaken is protected by the flagman going back with two torpedoes and, when necessary, lighted fusees; when called in he leaves the torpedoes and a lighted fusee. The front is protected the same way when necessary.

32 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule S-88

Meeting Extra 530 West

Your order says Extra 812 East meet Extra 530 West at Granite. Westward trains are superior by direction. Which extra takes the siding?

  • Extra 530 West, because it is the opposing train
  • Extra 812 East, the train in the inferior time-table direction
  • The one with the higher engine number
  • Whichever arrives first

Rule S-88: when two extras meet, the train in the inferior time-table direction takes the siding, unless otherwise provided. The TT&TO primer on Form S-A: neither train goes past Granite until both have arrived.

33 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 104

The siding switch

Your head brakeman lined the switch at [station] and the train pulled into the siding. Who is responsible for that switch now?

  • Nobody; leave it open for the next train
  • The engineman
  • The section foreman
  • You, the conductor: it must be lined back for the main track

Rule 104: conductors are responsible for the position of switches used by them and their crews, except where switch tenders are stationed. A switch must not be left open for another train unless a member of that train's crew is in charge of it.

34 · 1949 run, on the road · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 99

Slow on the grade

Extra 812 East is crawling up the grade below Granite, and a superior train may come up behind you while you are still moving. How does the flagman protect the rear?

  • He drops lighted fusees at proper intervals
  • He goes back and places two torpedoes while the train keeps moving
  • None is needed while the train is moving
  • The engineman sounds — o o o every mile

Rule 99: a moving train that may be overtaken is protected by the flagman dropping lighted fusees at proper intervals. Torpedoes are for a stopped train.

35 · 1949 run, on the road · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 251

Block signals ahead

From Granite east the time-table names the track as governed by block signals for trains in the same direction. What decides how you run ahead of No 2 there?

  • A train order for each block
  • Superiority by class, as before
  • The block signal indications, which supersede superiority
  • Whoever reaches the next signal first

Rule 251: on designated tracks, trains run with reference to other trains in the same direction by block signals, whose indications supersede the superiority of trains.

36 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule S-89

Backing into the siding

The west switch here is blocked by a car, so you must back into the siding from the east end. What does Rule S-89 require?

  • Get a train order first
  • Nothing, if the superior train is not in sight
  • Protect the train as prescribed by Rule 99
  • Sound — — o — while backing

Rule S-89: if the inferior train must back in, it is protected as prescribed by Rule 99, unless otherwise provided.

37 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 82

A very late train

The operator says No 3, a regular train, is more than 12 hours behind its schedule at this station. What is its standing now?

  • It became an extra automatically
  • It has lost both right and schedule and may move only by train order
  • It keeps its schedule but loses right
  • It runs on its schedule at restricted speed

Rule 82: a regular train more than 12 hours behind its time at any station loses both right and schedule.

38 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 94

A disabled train

Word comes of an eastbound freight disabled ahead and unable to move. If needed, your train may…

  • Become a work extra
  • Pass it if practicable, and if necessary take its schedule and orders
  • Push it to the next siding
  • Wait until the dispatcher annuls its orders

Rule 94: pass the disabled train if practicable; if necessary assume its schedule and take its train orders, then report from the next point of communication.

39 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule S-71

What makes a train superior?

The operator quizzes you while you wait. On single track, how is one train superior to another?

  • By class only
  • By direction, then class, then right
  • By engine number
  • By right, class or direction; right, given by train order, beats class or direction

Rule S-71: right is conferred by train order, class and direction by time-table. Right is superior to class or direction, and direction counts only between trains of the same class.

40 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule S-72

Same class, opposite ways

No 1 West and an eastward passenger, both first class, are due to meet. With nothing in the orders, which is superior?

  • Neither; they need a meet order
  • No 1: the time-table makes westward trains superior between trains of the same class
  • The eastward train, which is running late
  • Whichever left its terminal first

Rule S-72: trains in the direction specified by the time-table are superior to trains of the same class in the opposite direction. On the Kestrel Valley that is westward.

41 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 72

First and second class

No 1 is first class and No 21 is second class. Which is superior?

  • No 1: first class is superior to second
  • No 21, being a freight
  • They are equal; direction decides
  • Whichever is closer to its schedule

Rule 72: trains of the first class are superior to those of the second, second to third, and so on.

42 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 85

Sections passing

First 2 is delayed here, and Second 2 wants to go around it. What must happen first?

  • First 2 takes down its green flags
  • Second 2 gets a train order from the dispatcher
  • Second 2 waits 10 minutes
  • The two sections exchange train orders, signals and numbers

Rule 85: a section must not pass another section of the same schedule without first exchanging train orders, signals and numbers with it, and the change is reported from the next point of communication.

43 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 92

Ready early

No 2 is ready to leave here four minutes before its schedule time. May it go?

  • No; a train must not leave a station before its schedule leaving time
  • Yes, first-class trains may run early
  • Yes, if no opposing train is due
  • Yes, if the dispatcher says so by phone

Rule 92: a train must not leave a station in advance of its schedule leaving time.

44 · 1949 run, at a station · TT&TO primer · Appendix

Before you leave

A TT&TO crew must know four things before departure: its own schedule if regular, the superior trains due, whether they have arrived or left, and…

  • The name of the next operator
  • The tonnage of the train behind
  • Whether it can make the next meeting point before a superior train is due
  • Whether the next office is open

TT&TO primer appendix: your schedule, the superior trains due, whether they have arrived or left, and whether you can make the next meeting point before a superior train is due.

45 · Signals run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 251

Signals and superiority

The time-table names this track as governed by block signals for trains in the same direction. How do you run with respect to No 2 ahead of you?

  • By superiority: No 2 is first class
  • By the block signal indications, which supersede the superiority of trains
  • By the time-table times, keeping 5 minutes behind
  • By train order only

Rule 251: on designated tracks, trains run with reference to other trains in the same direction by block signals, whose indications supersede the superiority of trains.

Train orders 20

46 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 221

The train order board

Coming into [station], the semaphore at the open office shows its blade horizontal.

  • Proceed: it is only a block signal
  • Slow down and take orders on the fly
  • Stop: an operator is on duty, and you must not leave without a Clearance Form A
  • Whistle — — and keep going

Rule 221: the train order signal shows stop while an operator is on duty, and trains must not leave without a Clearance Form A. The semaphore guide adds that a horizontal blade is always stop.

47 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 211

Check the clearance

The clearance lists Nos [order numbers], but you hold Nos [order numbers]. What do you do?

  • Cross out the number and write the right one in
  • Do not leave; have the operator correct it with the dispatcher
  • Leave and report it from the next office
  • Leave; the orders in hand are what count

Rule 211: Clearance Form A is filled out without erasure or alteration, and conductors, enginemen and firemen must see that its information matches the orders received.

48 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 211

Check the clearance

The clearance lists Nos [order numbers] and you hold Nos [order numbers]. Who on your crew must check that they match?

  • Only the conductor
  • Only the engineman
  • The conductor, the engineman and the fireman
  • The operator alone

Rule 211: conductors, enginemen and firemen, and trainmen when practicable, must see that the information on Clearance Form A matches the train orders received.

49 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Form E

Order No [order no]

“[order text].” What does this order do for you?

  • Ignore [train] until Ironton
  • Run with respect to [train]'s schedule [n] minutes later
  • Wait at [station] for [train]
  • You now have right over [train]

Form E, a time order: any train receiving it runs with respect to the later time exactly as it would to the regular schedule. The time-table on the right now shows the new times in red.

50 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 206

How the operator names you

The operator here asks how your train will be named in any order. What is right?

  • East Extra 812
  • Extra 812 East
  • No 812 East
  • Work Extra 812

Rule 206: extras are named by engine number and direction. Work extras are “Work Extra” and the engine number.

51 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 220

How long an order lasts

The fireman asks how long an order you hold stays in force.

  • 12 hours after it was issued
  • Until it is fulfilled, superseded or annulled
  • Until midnight
  • Until you reach Ironton

Rule 220: a train order is in effect until fulfilled, superseded or annulled. Orders are numbered each day from midnight (Rule 203), but that does not end them.

52 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Form S-C

A right-over order

The operator reads you another crew's order: “No 21 has right over Extra 640 East Granite to Hollis.” If they meet at Granite or Hollis, which train takes the siding?

  • Extra 640 East, the inferior train
  • Neither; they wait for a meet order
  • The first-named train, No 21, unless the order says otherwise
  • Whichever arrives last

Form S-C: the first-named train holds the right, and at either named point it takes the siding unless the order says otherwise.

53 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 207

On the wire

Standing at the office, you hear the dispatcher call: “31, East, copy 3.” What is he doing?

  • Asking for three clearances
  • Calling train No 31 east
  • Giving order number 31
  • Sending a train order with signal 31, direction East, three copies

Rule 207: the transmitting signal is “31” or “19”, then the direction, then the number of copies, given to each office addressed.

54 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 211

The wire goes down

The operator has all your orders complete, but the wire fails before the dispatcher gives the OK on the clearance.

  • He gives you a verbal OK and you go
  • He may deliver them with the clearance marked “Wire has failed”
  • The orders are void and must be sent again
  • You must wait until the wire is restored

Rule 211: if all orders for the train are complete, the operator may deliver them with Clearance Form A marked “Wire has failed”, acted on as though OK had been given.

55 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Form S-H

A work extra ahead

The operator reads you the work train's order: “Eng 292 works extra 7 00 am until 5 00 pm between Elk Gap and Fenwick.” Inside those limits, who protects against your extra?

  • Nobody; work extras have right over extras
  • The dispatcher, by holding you at Elk Gap
  • The work extra protects itself against extras in both directions
  • You must flag through the limits

Form S-H: within the working limits the work extra, standing or moving, protects itself against extra trains in both directions, and it must clear the time of regular trains.

56 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Form L

An annulled order

The operator says order 9 was annulled this morning. May the dispatcher issue a new order under number 9 later today?

  • No; an annulled order is never reissued under its number
  • Only for extras
  • Yes, if the dispatcher initials it
  • Yes, once the annulment is delivered

Form L: an annulled order must not be reissued under its original number. Orders are numbered each day from midnight (Rule 203).

57 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Form S-P

Instead of

An order reads “No 21 meet Extra 640 East at Hollis instead of Granite.” What has happened?

  • An earlier meet at Granite is superseded; the meet is now at Hollis
  • No 21 waits at Granite, then at Hollis
  • The Granite order is annulled and no meet remains
  • There are now two meets, at Granite and Hollis

Form S-P: the words “instead of” supersede an order or part of one. A superseded order is not reissued under its number.

58 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Form G

And return

Another crew's order reads “Eng 640 run extra Ironton to Cobb and return to Hollis.” Where must Extra 640 go before turning back?

  • All the way to Cobb
  • Anywhere between Ironton and Cobb
  • Only to the first open office
  • To Hollis, then back

Form G: “…and return” means the extra must go all the way out to the far point before returning.

59 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 222

The operator's report

As you leave, the operator picks up the phone to the dispatcher. What must he report about your train?

  • Its time of arrival and departure, and the direction of an extra
  • Its tonnage and crew names
  • Nothing, unless you had orders
  • Only the number of cars

Rule 222: operators promptly record and report the time of arrival and departure of all trains and the direction of extra trains.

60 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Form S-C (2)

Right over a regular train

The operator reads you another crew's order: “Extra 640 East has right over No 1 Cobb to Granite.” What must No 1 do?

  • Clear Extra 640 East's time by 5 minutes
  • Not go beyond Granite until Extra 640 East has arrived
  • Take the siding at Granite on arrival
  • Wait at Cobb for Extra 640 East

Form S-C (2): the regular train must not go beyond the point last named until the extra has arrived, unless authorized by train order.

61 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Form S-C (3)

Right over, with a wait

The operator reads you another crew's order: “Extra 640 East has right over Extra 70 West Ashby to Ironton and wait at Elk Gap until 8 10 am.” What does it mean for Extra 640 East?

  • Extra 70 West must wait at Elk Gap until 8:10
  • It must not pass Elk Gap before 8:10 unless Extra 70 West has arrived
  • It must reach Elk Gap by 8:10
  • It stops at Elk Gap and waits for Extra 70 West whatever the time

Form S-C with wait times: the first-named extra must not pass the waiting points before the times given unless the second-named extra has arrived. The second-named extra clears those times by not less than five minutes.

62 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Form D

Right over, same direction

The operator reads you another crew's order: “No 2 has right over Extra 640 East Cobb to Granite,” with no times. What must Extra 640 East do?

  • Clear No 2's time by 10 minutes
  • Not leave Cobb ahead of No 2
  • Nothing; No 2 is behind it
  • Take the siding at Granite

Form D gives right over a train in the same direction. If no time is given, the second-named train must not leave the first-named point ahead of the first-named train.

63 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Form F

Running sections

An order reads “Eng 20 display signals and run as First 2 Ashby to Ironton. Eng 25 run as Second 2 Ashby to Ironton.” Which engine carries the green flags?

  • Both engines
  • Eng 20, First 2
  • Eng 25, Second 2
  • Neither; the order replaces the flags

Form F runs sections. Rule 20: every section except the last displays two green flags, two green lights at night, to show another section follows.

64 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Form D-H

Work extra on double track

An order lets Work Extra 292 work on Main 1 between Hollis and Ironton. Against which trains does it protect itself?

  • Extras in both directions on both tracks
  • Extras moving with the current of traffic on Main 1; it still clears regular trains
  • Nobody; it holds the track
  • Regular trains only

Form D-H: the work extra protects itself within the limits against extras moving with the current of traffic on the named track, and the time of regular trains must be cleared.

65 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 203

Order numbers

The operator notes today's orders started again at No 1. When does the numbering restart?

  • At each shift change
  • At the start of each time-table
  • Each day at midnight
  • Never; numbers run through the year

Rule 203: train orders are numbered consecutively each day, beginning at midnight.

Signals & whistles 31

66 · 1949 run, on the road · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 14(l)

Crossing at grade

A public road crosses the line ahead at grade. Which whistle does the engineman sound?

  • — —
  • — — o —, prolonged or repeated until the crossing is reached
  • — o o o
  • o o o

Rule 14(l): — — o — approaching public crossings at grade. — o o o calls the flagman to protect the rear; o o o when standing is back; — — is release brakes, proceed.

67 · 1949 run, on the road · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 12(b)

A signal from the ground

A section foreman beside the track holds his flag out horizontally at arm's length.

  • Back up
  • Proceed
  • Reduce speed
  • Stop

Rule 12: held horizontally at arm's length is reduced speed. Swung at right angle to the track is stop, raised and lowered vertically is proceed, swung in a circle is back.

68 · 1949 run, on the road · Signals guide · Signal signage

Automatic block signal

In the automatic block between stations, a signal with a number plate shows stop.

  • Pass at reduced speed without stopping
  • Stop, then proceed at restricted speed
  • Wait 5 minutes, then proceed at track speed
  • Wait for the dispatcher's permission

A number plate marks a permissive signal: after stopping, you may proceed at restricted speed. An A plate or no plate is absolute.

69 · 1949 run, on the road · Signals guide · Signal signage

Stop on the hill

Halfway up the grade, an automatic signal with a G plate and a number plate shows stop.

  • Pass it at restricted speed without stopping
  • Pass it at track speed
  • Stop and wait for permission
  • Stop, then proceed at restricted speed

A G plate marks a grade signal: a train may pass it at restricted speed without stopping.

70 · 1949 run, on the road · Signals guide · Signal signage

A P plate

The signal ahead carries a P plate and shows stop.

  • A passenger station is ahead
  • A pilot is required
  • It is a permissive signal; after stopping, proceed at restricted speed
  • There is a detector in the block, such as high water or a slide, and the crew must inspect it

A P plate marks a protective signal: a detector in the block that the crew must check.

71 · 1949 run, on the road · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 12a

A lamp across the track

Ahead, a man on the ground swings a lamp at right angle to the track.

  • Back up
  • Proceed
  • Reduce speed
  • Stop

Rule 12(a): swung at right angle to the track means stop.

72 · 1949 run, on the road · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 12c

Up and down

The head brakeman at the switch raises and lowers his lamp vertically.

  • Back up
  • Proceed
  • Release brakes
  • Stop

Rule 12(c): raised and lowered vertically means proceed.

73 · 1949 run, on the road · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 14(a)

One short

The engineman sounds one short blast: o.

  • Acknowledge
  • Apply brakes, stop
  • Back up
  • Release brakes, proceed

Standard Code Rule 14(a): one short is apply brakes, stop. The GCOR uses one long (—) for brakes applied when stopped.

74 · 1949 run, on the road · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 14(b)

Two longs

After the stop, the engineman sounds — —.

  • Approaching a crossing
  • Back up
  • Flagman protect rear
  • Release brakes, proceed

Rule 14(b): two longs mean release brakes, proceed. The same in the GCOR.

75 · 1949 run, on the road · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 14(h)

Three shorts, standing

Standing in the siding, the engineman sounds o o o.

  • Apply brakes
  • Back
  • Flagman go out
  • Proceed

Rule 14(h): o o o when standing means back, the answer to hand signal 12(d). When running it answers the communicating signal.

76 · 1949 run, on the road · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 14(c)

Long and three shorts

The train stops short on the main and the engineman sounds — o o o.

  • Approaching a crossing
  • Back up
  • Flagman protect rear of train
  • Release brakes, proceed

Rule 14(c): — o o o calls the flagman to protect the rear of the train.

77 · 1949 run, on the road · Signals guide · Definitions

Aspect and indication

The fireman calls out “yellow.” Is he naming the aspect or the indication?

  • Both; they are the same
  • The aspect: what the signal looks like. The indication is what it tells you to do
  • The indication
  • The name of the signal rule

Aspect is what you see; indication is what it tells you (stop, approach, clear); the name is the railroad's label, usually by rule number.

78 · 1949 run, on the road · Signals guide · Definitions

Route or speed?

The Kestrel Valley's signals tell you which route you are lined for and how clear the blocks are, and speeds come from the time-table. What is that system?

  • APB
  • Cab signaling
  • Route signaling
  • Speed signaling

Route signaling gives the route and the state of the blocks ahead; diverging speeds come from the time-table. Speed signaling tells you how fast to go past the signal.

79 · 1949 run, on the road · Signals guide · Definitions

Opposing signals

On this stretch, once you pass the head block signal at a siding, every opposing signal goes to stop through to the next siding. What system is that?

  • An interlocking
  • APB, Absolute Permissive Block
  • CTC
  • Plain ABS

APB: when a train passes a head block at a siding, all opposing signals go to stop through to the head block at the next siding. ABS has the blocks without that rule.

80 · 1949 run, on the road · Signals guide · Signal chart

A green signal

The next block signal shows a single green.

  • Approach: next block is unoccupied
  • Clear: next two blocks are unoccupied
  • Proceed at restricted speed
  • Proceed on the diverging route

Basic Signal Indication Chart: green is Clear, next two blocks are unoccupied. Yellow is Approach, next block is unoccupied.

81 · 1949 run, on the road · Signals guide · Signal chart

A yellow signal

The block signal ahead shows a single yellow.

  • Approach: next block is unoccupied
  • Clear: next two blocks are unoccupied
  • Diverging route
  • Stop and proceed

Basic Signal Indication Chart: yellow is Approach, next block is unoccupied. Green is Clear, next two blocks are unoccupied.

82 · 1949 run, on the road · 1949 Standard Code · Fixed Signals

How signals show

Which of these is NOT a way the Standard Code says a fixed signal can show its aspect?

  • By flashing of lights
  • By the color of lights
  • By the position of semaphore arms
  • By the sound of a bell

Standard Code: fixed signal aspects are shown by position of semaphore arms, color of lights, position of lights, flashing of lights, or a combination.

83 · 1949 run, at a station · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 12(d)

Hand signal

The head brakeman on the ground swings his lamp vertically in a circle at right angle to the track. What does he want?

  • Apply air brakes
  • Back up
  • Proceed
  • Stop

Rule 12(d): swung vertically in a circle at right angle to the track is back. The engineman answers with o o o (Rule 14(h)).

84 · Modern run · GCOR · 5.8.2

Men on the track

Box 12 is in your warrant. Rounding a curve you see a track gang ahead at Cobb. What whistle signal?

  • — — o —
  • — o, then o o at intervals until the head end has passed them
  • A succession of short sounds
  • None; Box 12 replaces the whistle

GCOR 5.8.2 (8): — o approaching men or equipment, regardless of whistle prohibitions; then o o intermittently until the head end has passed. It cannot be replaced by radio.

85 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · 5.8.2(7)

Crossing at 40 MPH

You are running at 40 MPH toward a public crossing. When does the engineer start the crossing whistle?

  • 10 seconds before the crossing
  • A quarter mile before the crossing
  • At least 15 but not more than 20 seconds before the crossing
  • At the whistle sign, whatever the speed

GCOR 5.8.2(7): at 45 MPH or less, start at least 15 but not more than 20 seconds before entering the crossing. Over 45 MPH, start at or about the sign but not more than 1/4 mile before. The pattern is — — o —, held until the engine occupies the crossing.

86 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · 5.8.2

Short blasts ahead

From a train on the passing track ahead you hear a long succession of short whistle sounds.

  • Answer o o and continue
  • Continue at restricted speed
  • Sound the same signal back
  • Stop until it is safe to proceed

GCOR 5.8.2 (1): a succession of short sounds warns of persons or livestock on the track or an emergency such as a derailment. Crews on other trains who hear it must stop until it is safe.

87 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · 5.8.3

The whistle fails

The horn on the lead unit quits and no other unit can lead. How do you go on?

  • At restricted speed only
  • Normally, with the headlight on bright
  • Not at all; wait for a rescue engine
  • With the bell ringing continuously, stopping before each public crossing unless the gates are down or no traffic is near

GCOR 5.8.3: continue with the bell ringing and stop before each public crossing so a crew member can warn traffic, unless the gates are fully down or no traffic is approaching or stopped.

88 · Modern run, on the road · Signals guide · Route indications

Two heads at the junction

The interlocking signal at the junction shows red over yellow.

  • Approach on the main route
  • Diverging Approach: the OS block and the next block are unoccupied, but the block after that is occupied
  • Restricting
  • Stop: there is red on the mast

It is not red unless it is all red. Red over yellow is Diverging Approach: the OS block and the next block are unoccupied but the next block after that is occupied.

89 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · 5.8.1

Before moving

You are ready to pull out of the siding at Hollis. What does the engineer do before moving?

  • Nothing; the radio call is enough
  • Ring the bell
  • Sound — — o —
  • Sound a succession of short sounds

GCOR 5.8.1: ring the bell before moving (except momentary stop-and-start switching), approaching men or equipment, and approaching public crossings.

90 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · 5.8.2(7)

Crossing at 50 MPH

On the tangent past Fenwick you are at 50 MPH, approaching a public crossing. When does the crossing whistle start?

  • 15 to 20 seconds before the crossing
  • At or about the crossing sign, but not more than 1/4 mile before the crossing
  • Half a mile before the crossing
  • When the crossing comes into view

GCOR 5.8.2(7): over 45 MPH, start at or about the sign, but not more than 1/4 mile before. At 45 MPH or less, start 15 to 20 seconds before.

91 · Signals run · 1949 Standard Code · Fixed Signals

How a signal speaks

The road foreman asks how the Standard Code says a fixed signal can show its aspect.

  • By a sign giving the speed in miles per hour
  • By color of lights only, day and night
  • By position of semaphore arms, color of lights, position of lights, flashing of lights, or a combination of these
  • By the position of semaphore arms only

Standard Code, Fixed Signals: aspects may be shown by position of semaphore arms, color of lights, position of lights, flashing of lights, or a combination of color, position and flashing.

92 · Signals run · 1949 Standard Code · Rules 289, 291

Stop, or Stop and proceed?

Two signals ahead both show two horizontal red arms. What tells you whether one is Stop and proceed (Rule 291) rather than Stop (Rule 292)?

  • A letter plate, marker light, shape of arm, or a combination of these
  • Its height above the rail
  • The color of its lights only
  • The number of arms

Rules 289 and 291: designate by a letter plate, a marker light, the shape of the arm, or a combination of these. The Code draws Stop with three, two or one arms.

93 · Signals run · Signals guide · Definitions

Route or speed?

These signals tell you which route you are lined for and how clear the blocks are ahead; diverging speeds come from the timetable. What system is that?

  • Absolute permissive block
  • Cab signaling
  • Route signaling
  • Speed signaling

Signals guide: route signaling tells you the route and the state of the blocks ahead; speed through diverging routes is in the timetable. Speed signaling tells you how fast to go.

94 · Signals run · Signals guide · Definitions

Opposing signals

Past the head block signal at Dunmore, every opposing signal goes to Stop through to the head block at the next siding. What system is that?

  • ABS, Automatic Block Signals, with no opposing rule
  • An interlocking, worked from a tower
  • APB, Absolute Permissive Block
  • CTC, set by a dispatcher

Signals guide: under APB, when a train passes a head block, all opposing signals are set to stop up to and including the head block at the next siding.

95 · Signals run · Signals guide · Signal placement

Where the CP signals stand

At CP Hollis, where is the facing point signal?

  • At the clearance point
  • Just clear of the switch points
  • On a dwarf beside the siding
  • Opposite the next intermediate signal

Signals guide, typical signal placement in CTC: the facing point signal is just clear of the switch points; trailing point signals are at the clearance point; a dwarf is often used on the siding.

96 · Yard job · GCOR · 5.8.2

Car men on track 3

Car men are working on track 3, next to the engine track. The engine is ready to move. What does the engineer do first?

  • Ask the train dispatcher for permission
  • Move at restricted speed without a signal
  • Nothing; the engine track is not main track
  • Sound the required whistle signal before moving

GCOR 5.8.2: when other employees are working in the immediate area, sound the required whistle signal before moving.

Semaphores 7

97 · 1949 run, on the road · Semaphores guide

Semaphore ahead

A semaphore block signal ahead shows its blade horizontal.

  • Approach, prepared to stop at the next signal
  • Clear
  • It depends on whether it is upper or lower quadrant
  • Stop

A horizontal semaphore blade is always stop, upper or lower quadrant.

98 · 1949 run, on the road · Semaphores guide

An old lower-quadrant blade

The fireman notes the next signal is a lower-quadrant semaphore. Why is a lower-quadrant blade not fail-safe?

  • If the mechanism fails, gravity drops the blade toward a proceed position
  • It can show only two positions
  • Its lamp burns out easily
  • Snow freezes it at stop

On a lower-quadrant signal the blade drops to clear (0°, 30°, 60°), so a broken linkage can turn stop into approach or clear. Upper-quadrant blades rise (0°, 45°, 90°).

99 · 1949 run, on the road · Semaphores guide

Behind the blade

The colored glass lenses on a semaphore are the roundels. What holds them?

  • The blade
  • The housing
  • The lamp
  • The spectacle

Semaphore parts: blade, roundels (the lenses), spectacle (holds the roundels), lamp, actuating mechanism, housing.

100 · 1949 run, on the road · Semaphores guide

Upper quadrant

The signal ahead is an upper-quadrant semaphore. Through what positions does its blade move?

  • 0° and 90° only
  • 0°, 30° and 60°, dropping
  • 0°, 45° and 90°, rising from horizontal
  • 0°, 60° and 90°

Upper-quadrant blades rise to clear through 0°, 45° and 90°, and came about around 1900. Lower-quadrant blades drop through 0°, 30° and 60°.

101 · 1949 run, on the road · Semaphores guide

Fixed at 45 degrees

Before the river bridge stands a semaphore whose blade never moves from 45°. What is it?

  • A broken signal to report
  • A single-position signal: a permanent approach warning of something ahead
  • A stop signal
  • A train order board

Single-position semaphores were fixed at 45° as a permanent warning of something ahead such as a bridge, commonly for a restricting indication.

102 · 1949 run, on the road · Semaphores guide

Old signals

The fireman says these semaphores are as old as the railroad. When was the semaphore patented?

  • Around 1900
  • In the 1840s
  • In the 1870s
  • In the 1930s

The semaphore was patented in the 1840s and first lit by kerosene, later by electric bulbs. The upper quadrant came around 1900.

103 · Signals run · Semaphores guide

Arms up

These semaphores raise their arms to show proceed. What kind are they?

  • Lower quadrant: the blade drops to show proceed
  • Single-position signals
  • Smashboard signals
  • Upper quadrant: the blade rises from horizontal to 45° and 90°

Semaphores guide: an upper-quadrant blade rises through 45° and 90°; a lower-quadrant blade drops toward proceed, so it is not fail-safe.

Yard limits 11

104 · 1949 run · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 93

Into yard limits

You pass the yard limit sign at Ironton. A switch engine may be working on the main. At what speed do you run?

  • Any speed, with the bell ringing
  • Maximum authorized speed; you have no more trains to clear
  • Restricted speed, not over 20 MPH
  • Yard speed, unless the main track is known to be clear

Standard Code Rule 93: within yard limits, protection against ____ class (left blank in the Code; the TT&TO primer fills in second class), extra trains and engines is not required; they move at yard speed unless the main track is known to be clear. The 20 MPH figure is GCOR 6.27, not the Standard Code.

105 · 1949 run · Yard Limits guide

Who is in charge here?

Inside the Ironton yard limits, who is in charge of the moves if a yardmaster is on duty?

  • The conductor of the first train there
  • The dispatcher
  • The engineer of the longest train
  • The yardmaster

Yard Limits guide: the yardmaster or agent if one is on duty; otherwise generally the conductor or switch crew foreman of the first train there.

106 · Modern run · GCOR · 6.13

Moving up to the limit sign

You pull up the main inside the Ashby yard limits toward the yard limit sign. There is no block signal. At what speed?

  • 10 MPH
  • Maximum authorized speed
  • Restricted speed
  • Yard speed, unless the main is known to be clear

GCOR 6.13: within yard limits, movements are made at restricted speed unless a block signal shows something more favorable than Approach. “Yard speed unless known clear” is the Standard Code wording.

107 · Modern run · GCOR · 6.13

Block signal at Ironton

Inside Ironton yard limits a block signal shows Approach (yellow). At what speed may you move past it?

  • Any speed, since you have a warrant
  • Prepared to stop at the next signal, at track speed
  • Restricted speed
  • Yard speed

GCOR 6.13: within yard limits, restricted speed unless the block signal indication is more favorable than Approach. Approach is not.

108 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · 6.13

Yard limits in CTC

On the next subdivision, the yard limits lie in CTC territory. Who must authorize a move on the main track there?

  • Nobody; yard limit rules apply
  • The conductor of the first train there
  • The control operator
  • The yardmaster

GCOR 6.13: in CTC territory the control operator must authorize any main track movement, even within yard limits.

109 · Modern run, on the road · Yard Limits guide

Why yard limits?

The engineer asks why Ironton has yard limits at all.

  • So crews can use short stretches of main track without the dispatcher issuing many fast-changing orders or warrants
  • To allow higher speeds near the yard
  • To keep extras off the main
  • To mark where warrants are delivered

Yard Limits guide: many trains and engines need short stretches of main track, such as a yard ladder joined to the main. Yard limits let them work without a stream of orders or warrants.

110 · Yard job · GCOR · 6.13

Onto Main 1

From the lead you head out onto Main 1, inside the yard limits. The block signal at the lead shows Clear. Must the move be made at restricted speed?

  • No, but not over 10 MPH
  • No: the movement is under a block signal more favorable than Approach
  • Yes, until the job passes the east yard limit sign
  • Yes: every movement inside yard limits is at restricted speed

GCOR 6.13: within yard limits, all movements at restricted speed unless under a block signal more favorable than Approach. Clear is more favorable.

111 · Yard job · GCOR · 6.13

Onto Main 1

From the lead you head out onto Main 1, inside the yard limits. The block signal at the lead shows Approach. Must the move be made at restricted speed?

  • No: any block signal lifts the yard limit speed
  • No: Approach means the next block is clear, so track speed
  • Only if a yardmaster is on duty
  • Yes: only a signal better than Approach lifts restricted speed

GCOR 6.13: within yard limits, all movements at restricted speed unless under a block signal more favorable than Approach. An Approach does not lift it.

112 · Yard job · GCOR · 6.13

A train behind you

While the job works on Main 1, the eastward passenger train comes around the curve behind you on Main 1. What does the job do?

  • Ask the dispatcher for a track warrant to stay on Main 1
  • Get out of the way: engines give way to trains as they approach and must not delay passenger trains
  • Keep working: inside yard limits nobody protects against anybody
  • Light a fusee so the train stops behind the cut

GCOR 6.13: trains and engines may use the main track without protecting against other trains or engines, but engines give way to trains as they approach and must not delay passenger trains.

113 · Yard job · GCOR · 6.13

Against the current

The Kestrel Feed spur leaves Main 2, the westward main. To reach it, the job must run east on Main 2. What does that move need?

  • A flagman 1 mile ahead of the movement
  • Authorization or protection by track warrant, track bulletin, yardmaster or other authorized employee
  • Nothing: yard limits allow any move on the main track
  • Permission from the control operator at CP Ironton East

GCOR 6.13: within yard limits, movements against the current of traffic must not be made unless authorized or protected by track warrant, track bulletin, yardmaster or other authorized employee. Ironton's control operator governs only the CTC east of the CP.

114 · Yard job · GCOR · 6.13

Toward CP Ironton East

The yardmaster sends the 2 empties east to CP Ironton East for the eastward local. Past the CP the yard limits lie in CTC territory. Who must authorize the job's movement on the main track there?

  • No one: yard limits allow any main track movement
  • The conductor of the eastward local
  • The control operator
  • The yardmaster

GCOR 6.13: where yard limits are in effect in CTC territory, the control operator must authorize any movement on the main track.

Track warrants 24

115 · Modern run · GCOR · 14.8

Calling the dispatcher

At the yard limit sign you call the dispatcher for a track warrant. What do you tell him?

  • Only your train symbol; he works out the rest
  • The OK time you would like
  • What movements you will make and, when necessary, which tracks and how much time you need
  • Your train's tonnage and car count

GCOR 14.8: tell the dispatcher what movements will be made and, when necessary, which tracks and how much time is required.

116 · Modern run · GCOR · 14.9

The OK time

The dispatcher has given the OK time and his initials. What do you do now?

  • Read the box numbers back again
  • Tell the engineer to go; the warrant is good
  • Wait for a written copy at the next station
  • Write the OK time and initials on the warrant and repeat them

GCOR 14.9 step 4: the employee writes the OK time and initials and repeats them. A warrant is not in effect until the OK time is shown on it.

117 · Modern run · GCOR · 14.9

Copies

Who must have a copy of warrant 101?

  • Only the engineer, who runs the train
  • Only you, the conductor
  • The conductor and the engineer, each copy dated
  • The dispatcher keeps the only copy

GCOR 14.9: the conductor and the engineer each have a copy, every crew member must read and understand it, and the copy shows the date.

118 · Modern run · GCOR · 14.0 form

Box 5

Warrant 101 has its OK time, and Box 5 reads “Not in effect until [time].” It is [time]. May you leave now?

  • No; wait until [time], when the warrant takes effect
  • Yes, at restricted speed until [time]
  • Yes, if no train is in sight
  • Yes; the OK time puts it in effect

Box 5: Not in effect until the time shown. Box 6 is the other timing box: This authority expires at the time shown.

119 · Modern run · GCOR · 14.0 form

Box 15

Box 15 is checked on warrant 101: “Flag protection not required against following trains on the same track.” What does that tell you?

  • No other train is on the subdivision
  • The dispatcher protects your rear: you need not flag against following trains
  • You may back up without permission
  • You must flag against following trains

Box 15: flag protection not required against following trains on the same track. The TWC guide says a model railroad can drop it, along with Boxes 5, 6 and 12 to 14.

120 · Modern run · GCOR · 14.0 form

Joint with work train 292

Boxes 11 and 17 say you are joint with work train 292 between Birchwood and Cobb. How do you run there?

  • At maximum authorized speed; 292 will stay clear
  • At restricted speed: the limits are occupied by a train
  • Not over 30 MPH
  • Stop and wait for 292 to report clear

Box 11: between the points, make all movements at restricted speed; limits occupied by train. Box 17 carries other instructions such as “joint with”. GCOR 6.27: not over 20 MPH, able to stop within half the range of vision.

121 · Modern run · GCOR · 14.2

Where does warrant 101 end?

Dunmore is the last named point, and Box 10 tells you to clear the main track there. Where does your authority end?

  • At the Dunmore station sign
  • At the first siding switch at Dunmore, including it
  • At the last siding switch at Dunmore
  • At the next station, Elk Gap

GCOR 14.2: at the last named point, authority extends to and includes the first siding switch. First is last and last is first. GCOR 14.3: never foul a switch at either end where an opposing train may use it to clear.

122 · Modern run · Track Warrants guide · Selected rules

Into the siding

You head into the siding at Dunmore. The warrant does not govern the siding. How fast may you move in it?

  • At a speed that lets you stop within half the range of vision
  • Maximum authorized speed
  • Restricted speed under warrant 101
  • Yard speed

Track warrants govern only the main track. In sidings and other tracks, move at a speed that lets you stop within half the range of vision short of any obstruction or improperly lined switch (GCOR 6.28).

123 · Modern run · Track Warrants guide · Selected rules

Reporting clear

The engine is in the siding at Dunmore. When can you report clear of warrant 101's limits?

  • Now; the engine is clear
  • When 2211 West is in sight
  • When the engine passes the clearance point
  • When the whole train is off the main and the switch is lined back to normal

Clear of the limits means the whole train, not just the engine, clear of the limits and off the main track, with switches restored to normal (except within yard limits).

124 · Modern run · GCOR · 14.0 form

Box 7

Warrant 102 has its OK time. A headlight is coming: 2211 West is a mile out of Dunmore. May you pull out of the siding?

  • No. The warrant is not in effect until 2211 West has arrived at Dunmore
  • Yes, after whistling — o
  • Yes, at restricted speed
  • Yes; the OK time is on the warrant

Box 7: Not in effect until after arrival of the named train at the named point. Box 7 was used in the worked example for 844 West waiting on 2211 East.

125 · Modern run · Track Warrants guide · Worked example

The other warrant

2211 West has arrived at Dunmore, the end of its own warrant. What happens to that warrant now?

  • 2211 West reports clear of its limits, and the dispatcher voids its warrant
  • It passes to your train with warrant 102
  • It stays in effect until midnight
  • Nothing; the dispatcher keeps it open for the return trip

In the guide's worked example, 844 West's warrant is not in effect until after arrival of 2211 East at Olga Yard. When 2211 East arrives, its warrant 701 is reported clear and voided. Here 2211 West does the same at Dunmore. Unless a Box 6 time ends it sooner, a warrant stays in effect until the crew releases it.

126 · Modern run · GCOR · 14.2

The end of warrant 102

Granite is your last named point and Box 8, Hold main track at last named point, is checked. Where does your authority end?

  • At the first siding switch, including it
  • At the Granite station sign
  • At the last siding switch, including it
  • Short of the last siding switch at Granite, not including it

Box 8 extends the limit past the near switch, to but not including the last siding switch, so you hold the main while an opposing train uses the siding. GCOR 14.3: never foul that switch.

127 · Modern run · GCOR · 14.2

The end of warrant 102

Granite is your last named point. Where does your authority end?

  • At the first siding switch at Granite, including it
  • At the Granite depot
  • At the last siding switch at Granite, including it
  • At the next station, Hollis

GCOR 14.2: at the last named point, authority extends to and includes the first siding switch. First is last and last is first.

128 · Modern run · GCOR · 14.3

The far switch

Stopped at the end of warrant 102, the engineer asks whether he may pull ahead far enough to foul the far siding switch at Granite. An opposing train may use that switch to clear the main. May he?

  • No; a train must not foul a switch at either end of its limits where an opposing train may use it to clear
  • Yes, at restricted speed
  • Yes, if he stops short of the station sign
  • Yes, if he whistles — o first

GCOR 14.3: the train must not foul a switch at either end of its limits where an opposing train may use that switch to clear the main track. Box 8 already stops your limit short of that switch.

129 · Modern run · GCOR · 14.0 form

Box 2 or Box 4?

640 East, the Ironton local, is working the industries between Hollis and Ironton. Which box lets it move both ways in its limits?

  • Box 10, Clear main track at last named point
  • Box 2, Proceed from … to
  • Box 4, Work between
  • Box 7, Not in effect until after arrival of

Box 2 is one direction only; backing up needs permission for a reverse move. Box 4, Work between, gives movement in both directions for locals and work trains.

130 · Modern run · GCOR · 14.0 form

Box 13

Warrant 103 has Box 13, “Do not exceed 40 MPH between Granite and Hollis.” The engineer has the train up to 45 MPH on the tangent past Granite.

  • Bring it down to 40 MPH or less
  • Drop to restricted speed
  • Hold 45 until the next signal
  • Hold 45; the limit starts at Hollis

Boxes 13 and 14 set a speed limit between the named points; Box 13 here covers Granite to Hollis.

131 · Modern run · GCOR · 14.0 form

Boxes 13 and 14

Box 13 reads “Do not exceed 40 MPH between Granite and Hollis” and Box 14 “Do not exceed 30 MPH between Hollis and Ironton.” What is your limit now, between Hollis and Ironton?

  • 30 MPH, from Box 14
  • 40 MPH, from Box 13
  • Restricted speed, since two limits apply
  • The higher of the two, 40 MPH

Boxes 13 and 14 each limit speed between their own named points. Past Hollis, Box 14's 30 MPH applies.

132 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · 14.7

Reporting clear by a hand switch

You report clear of a warrant after leaving the main through a hand-operated switch, outside yard limits. What must you tell the dispatcher?

  • Nothing more; the switch is not his concern
  • Only that the train is clear
  • The position of the switch and that it is locked
  • The time you passed the switch

GCOR 14.7: outside yard or restricted limits, tell the dispatcher the switch position and that it is locked when reporting clear. He repeats it and you confirm.

133 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · 14.7

No caboose

There is no crew on the rear of KV 812 East. Which shows the dispatcher your whole train is clear of the limits?

  • A rear-end telemetry device, with air pressure on the head-end device showing brake pipe continuity
  • The engineer's word that the train felt complete
  • The head end passing the clearance point
  • The time since you passed the last station

GCOR 14.7 lists: a rear-end telemetry device with air pressure on the head-end device showing brake pipe continuity, an employee verifying the marker, a crew member seeing the rear car with the marker, an inspection while stopped, or matching axle counts from two detectors.

134 · Modern run, on the road · Track Warrants guide · Selected rules

Without a warrant

A hi-rail truck asks on the radio whether it can run on the main without a warrant. Who may occupy the main in TWC territory without one?

  • Anyone moving under 20 MPH
  • Nobody, except within yard limits or restricted limits
  • Passenger trains
  • Work extras

Outside yard (or restricted) limits, nobody occupies the main track in TWC territory without a warrant (GCOR 14.1).

135 · Modern run, on the road · Track Warrants guide · Selected rules

How long it lasts

Your warrant has no Box 6 time. How long does it stay in effect?

  • Until midnight
  • Until the dispatcher's shift ends
  • Until you reach the last named point
  • Until you release it

A track warrant stays in effect until the field employee releases it. Report clear of the limits as soon as practicable.

136 · Modern run, on the road · Track Warrants guide · Defined

What TWC is

The engineer, new to this line, asks what track warrant control is.

  • Operators hand up written orders at each station
  • Signals authorize each block
  • The dispatcher gives authority by voice; the crew copies it on a form, repeats it, and gets an OK time
  • The time-table authorizes each train

TWC authorizes trains, and men and equipment, across a specified territory. The dispatcher gives verbal instructions; the field employee copies them on a form and repeats them; the dispatcher gives an OK time.

137 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · 14.0 form

Box 9

Another crew's warrant has Box 9 checked with your train's symbol. What does Box 9 say?

  • Clear main track at last named point
  • Do not foul limits ahead of the named train
  • Joint with the named train
  • Not in effect until after arrival of the named train

Box 9: Do not foul limits ahead of __. Box 7 is Not in effect until after arrival of __ at __, and Box 10 is Clear main track at last named point.

138 · Modern run, on the road · Track Warrants guide · Selected rules

Model railroad warrants

The fireman runs TWC at his club. Which boxes does the TWC guide say a model railroad can drop?

  • Box 17 only
  • Boxes 2 and 3
  • Boxes 5 and 6 (times), 12 (men and equipment), 13 and 14 (speed) and 15
  • Boxes 7 and 8

The TWC guide says a model railroad can drop Box 12, Boxes 5 and 6, Boxes 13 and 14, and Box 15. The real line here uses them.

GCOR crew & speed 14

139 · Modern run · GCOR · 6.27

How long at restricted speed?

Box 12 puts you at restricted speed between Birchwood and Cobb. When may you resume speed?

  • When the foreman waves you by
  • When the leading wheels pass the end of the restriction
  • When the rear car passes the end
  • When you see a clear signal

GCOR 6.27: restricted speed applies until the leading wheels pass the point where it is no longer required. Not over 20 MPH, able to stop within half the range of vision.

140 · Modern run · GCOR · 1.47A

Approaching your limit

Dunmore is the end of your authority. When must you remind the engineer of it?

  • After passing the last station before it, and at least 2 miles before it
  • One mile before it
  • Only if he asks
  • When the Dunmore station sign comes into view

GCOR 1.47A: the conductor reminds the engineer when approaching the limits of authority after passing the last station, but at least 2 miles before.

141 · Modern run · GCOR · 1.43

Stalled in the tunnel

Your engine slips down to a stop in the tunnel at Elk Gap and cannot move promptly. What first?

  • Back out of the tunnel at once
  • Keep the engine running for heat and wait
  • Shut down the diesel, make a full service brake application, apply hand brakes and call the dispatcher
  • Sound a succession of short sounds

GCOR 1.43: shut down the diesel at once, make a full service brake application, apply hand brakes, and the dispatcher should be notified immediately.

142 · Modern run · GCOR · 6.25

Main 2, against the current

Box 3 sends you from Hollis to Ironton on Main 2, the westward main, because 640 East is working on Main 1. Why does that move need your warrant?

  • A move against the current of traffic must be authorized by track warrant or track bulletin
  • It does not; double track has no current of traffic outside CTC
  • Only because Main 2 is a siding
  • The engineer may decide without authority at restricted speed

GCOR 6.25: movement against the current of traffic must be authorized by track bulletin or track warrant, except under yard limits, restricted limits, track permits, signal protection by lining a switch in ABS, or DTC. Approach block and interlocking signals prepared to stop unless they show proceed.

143 · Modern run · GCOR · 1.46

Yarding the train

The Ironton yardmaster is on duty and tells you which track to yard on. Whose instructions do you follow?

  • The dispatcher's only
  • The engineer's
  • The yardmaster's
  • Your own, as conductor

GCOR 1.46: where a yardmaster is on duty, train, engine and yard crews comply with the yardmaster's instructions.

144 · Modern run · GCOR · 6.28

On the yard tracks

You shove the train onto yard track 4, off the main and outside any block system, at a speed that lets you stop within half the range of vision. Short of what must you be able to stop?

  • A train, engine, car, men or equipment, a stop signal, a derail or a switch lined wrong
  • Only another train
  • Only men on the track
  • Only the end of the track

GCOR 6.28: except on a main track or where a block system is in effect, move at a speed that allows stopping within half the range of vision short of a train, engine, car, men or equipment, stop signal, derail or improperly lined switch.

145 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · 5.6

A fusee on the track

A burning fusee lies between the rails of your track. Nobody is with it.

  • Ignore it; it is not a signal
  • Slow to 20 MPH and pass it
  • Stop and wait for a flagman
  • Stop, then go on at restricted speed for 1 mile beyond it

An unattended burning fusee: stop, then proceed at restricted speed for 1 mile beyond it. A fusee beyond the first rail of an adjacent track does not apply to your track.

146 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · 1.47C

Calling the signal

Passing a distant signal, you call it Approach and the engineer calls it Clear. How is it treated?

  • As the conductor calls it
  • As the engineer calls it: Clear
  • As the most restrictive indication observed: Approach
  • Stop and ask the dispatcher

GCOR 1.47C: crew members call each signal as soon as it is visible, and if they disagree, it is regarded as the most restrictive indication observed.

147 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · 1.47B

Special handling

There are two loads of steel plate on the head end. Who checks whether any cars need special handling?

  • Nobody; it is on the waybills
  • The dispatcher tells the engineer
  • The engineer checks with the conductor
  • The yardmaster at Ironton

GCOR 1.47B: the engineer must check with the conductor whether any cars need special handling.

148 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · 1.47A

Doubled up

The dispatcher combines your train with 640 East at Hollis. Both have conductors. Who is in charge?

  • The conductor of the leading train
  • The conductor with the most seniority
  • The dispatcher names one
  • The engineer of the lead unit

GCOR 1.47A: if trains combine, the senior conductor takes charge.

149 · Modern run, on the road · GCOR · 1.44, 1.45

Who directs whom

The Ironton operator relays a lineup to you. Whose direction does the operator work under?

  • Nobody's; operators work alone
  • The dispatcher's
  • The senior conductor's
  • The yardmaster's

GCOR 1.44 and 1.45: dispatchers supervise train movement; control operators and operators work under the dispatcher's direction for warrants, bulletins, lineups and train movements.

150 · Signals run · GCOR · 1.47C

Calling the signal

The engineer calls the next signal Approach; you see Clear. How is it treated?

  • As Clear, since the conductor supervises the train
  • As Stop until the dispatcher confirms it
  • As the most restrictive indication observed: Approach
  • As whichever the engineer called

GCOR 1.47C: if crew members disagree on the indication, treat it as the most restrictive one observed.

151 · Yard job · GCOR · 1.46

Whose list?

The yardmaster wants track 4 pulled first. The engineer would rather start with Kestrel Feed. Whose instructions does the yard job follow?

  • The conductor's alone, who supervises the job
  • The engineer's, who operates the engine
  • The train dispatcher's
  • The yardmaster's: where a yardmaster is on duty, train, engine and yard crews follow the yardmaster's instructions

GCOR 1.46: the yardmaster directly supervises yard crews; where a yardmaster is on duty, train, engine and yard crews follow the yardmaster's instructions.

152 · Yard job · GCOR · 6.28

Pulling the yard track

You pull the cars out of the yard track onto the yard lead. These are yard tracks, off the main and outside any block system. At what speed?

  • A speed that allows stopping within half the range of vision
  • Not over 10 MPH
  • Restricted speed, not over 20 MPH, looking out for broken rail
  • Yard speed, unless the track is known to be clear

GCOR 6.28: except on a main track or where a block system is in effect, move at a speed that allows stopping within half the range of vision short of a train, engine, car, men or equipment, stop signal, or derail or switch lined improperly.

At a Stop: the plates

Both signals runs · Signals guide · signage

A plate at Stop

The signal shows Stop and carries an A plate. What do you do?

  • Do not pass until permission is granted by whoever controls the signal
  • Inspect the protective device in the block
  • Pass at restricted speed without stopping
  • Stop, then proceed at restricted speed

An absolute signal: at stop, it may not be passed until permission is granted by the individual controlling the signal, usually a CTC dispatcher.

Both signals runs · Signals guide · signage

Number plate at Stop

The signal shows Stop and carries a number plate. What do you do?

  • Do not pass until permission is granted by whoever controls the signal
  • Get permission to proceed from the interlocking operator
  • Inspect the protective device in the block
  • Pass at restricted speed without stopping
  • Stop, then proceed at restricted speed

Number plate, usually the nearest milepost: after stopping, you may proceed at restricted speed.

Both signals runs · Signals guide · signage

G plate at Stop

The signal shows Stop and carries a G plate. What do you do?

  • Do not pass until permission is granted by whoever controls the signal
  • Get permission to proceed from the interlocking operator
  • Inspect the protective device in the block
  • Pass at restricted speed without stopping
  • Stop, then proceed at restricted speed

Grade signal, also with a number plate: it can be passed at restricted speed without stopping, which helps prevent a train from stalling on an upgrade.

Both signals runs · Signals guide · signage

SA plate at Stop

The signal shows Stop and carries an SA plate. What do you do?

  • Get permission to proceed from the interlocking operator
  • Inspect the protective device in the block
  • Pass at restricted speed without stopping
  • Stop, then proceed at restricted speed

Semi-automatic, usually in interlockings: an absolute and an ABS part. At stop, permission to proceed must be obtained from the interlocking operator.

Both signals runs · Signals guide · signage

P plate at Stop

The signal shows Stop and carries a P plate. What do you do?

  • Do not pass until permission is granted by whoever controls the signal
  • Get permission to proceed from the interlocking operator
  • Inspect the protective device in the block
  • Pass at restricted speed without stopping
  • Stop, then proceed at restricted speed

Protective signal: there is a protective device in the block, such as a high water or slide detector, that must be inspected by the train crew.

StationMPSidingNotes

Special instructions

  • Westward trains are superior to eastward trains of the same class.
  • One time shown is the leaving time (Rule 5).
  • Ashby and Ironton are inside yard limits.
  • Extras clear opposing regular trains by 5 minutes (Rule S-87).
  • Double track Hollis to Ironton: D- rules apply there.

The time order

At an open office the operator hands up a time order (Form E) on a westward regular train, for example:

Order No 11
No 1 run 20 mins late Ironton to Ashby

In the question, [train] is the train the order names and [n] its minutes: here No 1 and 20.

Track warrant 101

Track warrant no. 101 · copied at Ashby · to KV 812 East

2Proceed from Ashby to Dunmore on Main track
5Not in effect until [time]
10Clear main track at last named point
11Between Birchwood and Cobb make all movements at restricted speed. Limits occupied by train. some runs
12Between Birchwood and Cobb make all movements at restricted speed. Limits occupied by men or equipment. some runs
15Flag protection not required against following trains on the same track
17Other specific instructions: Joint with work train 292 between Birchwood and Cobb some runs

When you call for the warrant, the dispatcher sets Box 5 to the first 5-minute mark at least 12 minutes later. The question's two [time] values are that Box 5 time and the clock when you are ready to leave. Rows marked some runs are on the warrant in only some runs.
